questions.question: Given `type Dict = { [key: string]: number }`, what is `keyof Dict`?
questions.explanation: JavaScript converts numeric keys to strings, so a string index signature also accepts number keys. keyof therefore gives string | number.

questions.question: Given `const PLANS = ["basic", "silver", "gold"] as const;`, which type is the union "basic" | "silver" | "gold"?
questions.explanation: typeof lifts the value into a readonly tuple type, and indexing it with number gives the union of its element types. keyof PLANS and PLANS[number] are errors because PLANS is a value, not a type.

questions.question: Why is `getProperty<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]` better than `getProperty<T>(obj: T, key: keyof T): T[keyof T]`?
options: The separate K lets the compiler remember which key was passed, so the return type is that property's type rather than a union of all property types
The second version does not compile
It allows keys that are not in T
questions.explanation: With key: keyof T, every call returns the union of all value types. Capturing the key as its own type parameter K makes T[K] specific to the key used at each call.

questions.question: Why does `Object.keys(investor)` return `string[]` instead of `(keyof Investor)[]`?
options: Because Object.keys was written before TypeScript existed and was never updated
Because keyof does not work with objects
Because strict mode disables key inference
Because TypeScript is structural: the object may carry extra properties at runtime, so promising only the declared keys would be unsafe
questions.explanation: Any object with at least the declared properties is assignable to Investor, so it may have more keys at runtime. string[] is the honest type; cast with as (keyof Investor)[] only when you know the object is exact.
